name: AI for Stability and Shelf Life Prediction
blurb: Predicting long term stability from early data.
title: AI for Stability and Shelf Life Prediction
answer: Stability studies take years. Machine learning models that combine early stability time points with formulation and process data can predict long term behaviour, helping teams choose formulations sooner, though regulatory shelf life still rests on real stability data.

reading.body:
Machine learning can predict long term stability from early data, but it cannot set shelf life on its own.

The pattern is a split between prediction and evidence. Models combine early stability time points with formulation, packaging, and storage data to forecast long term behaviour, which lets teams flag formulations likely to fail and choose between them sooner. The inputs are historical stability results and process conditions, and the output is a ranking of candidates, not a registered expiry date.

This matters for AI because it shows where the technology actually sits in a regulated pipeline. Stability studies run for years, so the bottleneck is elapsed time rather than compute. A model that reads early time points and predicts the rest compresses the decision, not the study. The registration stability programme still runs, and shelf life still rests on stability data generated under regulatory guidance.

What the data does not cover is accuracy. No error rates, no validation results, and no count of formulations tested are given, so the size of the gain is unknown. It also does not say which regulatory bodies have accepted model output in a submission, only that shelf life rests on real data. The single dated development is a 2021 review describing such models, which establishes that the approach exists rather than that it is standard practice.

siblings.name: The FDA's View of AI in Drug Manufacturing

explainer:
Stability testing shows how a medicine's quality changes over time under different temperatures and humidity, and it sets the shelf life. Long term studies run for the full intended shelf life, often several years, which slows development and formulation choices.

Machine learning models trained on historical stability data, formulation properties and early time points can predict long term behaviour, flagging formulations likely to fail early. Accelerated stability modelling has long used similar ideas with physical chemistry. These predictions help development teams prioritise, but registration still rests on real stability data according to regulatory guidance, so models support decisions rather than replace studies.

What stability testing is for

Every medicine carries an expiry date and storage conditions, and both come from stability studies: batches stored at defined temperatures and humidities for months or years, tested at intervals for potency, impurities, dissolution and appearance. These studies are slow by design, because the point is to observe real degradation over real time. They are also a bottleneck, since a formulation change or a new market with a hotter climate may need a new study before a product can ship.

Where models help

AI and advanced statistics can learn from a company's accumulated stability data, thousands of batches across products with similar chemistry and packaging, to predict how a new formulation is likely to behave. That supports earlier decisions about which formulations to carry forward, which packaging to test, and where a product is at risk in a hot shipping lane. Models can also tighten the analysis of accelerated studies, where samples are stressed at higher temperatures to estimate long term behaviour faster.

What models cannot do yet

Regulators still require real time data to set an expiry date. A prediction can shorten the list of experiments and strengthen a filing, but it does not replace the study. Predictions are also only as good as the history they learn from, so a genuinely new chemistry or delivery form, where the company has no similar data, is exactly where the model is least reliable. Companies that use these tools well say so plainly in their filings and present the prediction alongside the measured data.

developments.text: A review in PMC described machine learning models predicting long term shelf life from initial stability data and process conditions.
